e.t: This Hebrew word refers to Beth Dagon, a place name rather than an ordinary descriptive word. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in the book of Joshua: twice in Joshua 15:41 and twice in Joshua 19:27. The English rendering preserves the name as “Beth” and “Dagon.” Without verse text, the name itself identifies the location, while the surrounding passage determines its role in each boundary or city-list setting.

This Hebrew word functions as a proper name, rendered “Bene.” It identifies a named location rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both within Joshua 19:45, so its use is limited and highly specific. The available lexical information does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this name. Its precise significance in Joshua 19:45 depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Its clearest scriptural pattern appears in creation passages, where God is the one who creates the heavens, earth, people, and other parts of the ordered world. The word occurs 54 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Genesis 1:1 and continuing through Malachi. It also functions as the predicate in passages that connect God with acts of creation.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “flesh,” referring to the bodily substance of a person or animal. It is used for physical flesh in descriptions of creation, living creatures, food, sacrifice, and bodily conditions. The word appears 270 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so its normal sense is broad but concrete: the physical body or its fleshly substance. Its use in passages about eating and offering flesh also shows that it can describe meat prepared for food or worship.

Gishpa is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, in Nehemiah 11:21. English Bibles render the name as “Gishpa.” Because the available information identifies the person only by name and does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, the name’s specific role in that verse cannot be explained further here.

Ohel is a personal name, referring to a particular individual rather than describing an action or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it appears only once, at 1 Chronicles 3:20, and English translations preserve it as “Ohel.” Because it is a name, its basic meaning is the person it identifies; the surrounding verse is needed to explain that individual’s place or significance in the passage.

Dumah is a Hebrew proper name, rendered as “Dumah,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, it occurs four times, each in a different verse. The name appears in Genesis, Joshua, 1 Chronicles, and Isaiah, so its precise referent is determined by the surrounding passage. A name alone does not tell the reader whether the passage identifies a person, place, or something else. The available lexical evidence supports retaining “Dumah” rather than translating it into another English concept.

Uzal is a Hebrew name, not a descriptive word with a supplied English definition. It appears three times in the Old Testament corpus and is rendered “Uzal.” Because the available information does not identify whether Uzal refers to a person, place, or people group in each passage, its exact referent must be determined from the surrounding verse and passage. The name occurs in Genesis 10:27, 1 Chronicles 1:21, and Ezekiel 27:19.

This Hebrew verb means “play” or “played.” It describes an action or behavior rather than a person or object, and its exact force depends on the sentence where it appears. The word occurs 93 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, so it is used broadly across that corpus. Its references extend from Genesis through Nahum, showing continued use across many periods of Israel’s Scriptures. The surrounding verse is needed to determine how the action is being described in a particular passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Eve.” It refers to the woman identified as the mother of all living and appears as a person’s name rather than a general description or action. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis: Genesis 3:20 and Genesis 4:1. Its use is closely connected with naming and with the birth of her son, placing the name within the Bible’s opening account of humanity and family beginnings.

This Hebrew verb expresses “pity”—a compassionate response toward someone in need or distress. It describes an action directed toward another person and can function as the main action in a sentence. The word occurs 24 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a recurring concern with whether someone will receive compassionate treatment. Its uses include people showing pity and declarations about withholding or extending it. The precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word means “cut.” It functions as an action word, describing what someone does when cutting something. Its basic sense concerns the act itself, while the surrounding verse identifies what is being cut and the purpose of the action. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing from Deuteronomy through Ezekiel. “Cut” captures its central meaning without requiring a broader range of translation terms.

This Hebrew word means “dream,” referring to a dream received or experienced during sleep. It is used 22 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within Daniel, and commonly describes the dream itself as something people recount, seek to understand, or connect with divine revelation. Its repeated use in Daniel 2 shows that a dream may be treated as meaningful and worthy of interpretation, while the surrounding passage determines its particular significance.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, this word refers to “Hannathon,” a named designation preserved in English rather than translated as an ordinary descriptive word. It occurs once, in Joshua 19:14, so its normal use is limited to that single occurrence. No broader lexical sense is established here; the word’s role is to identify Hannathon within the biblical text. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “peace.” It describes a settled condition or state and can function in a sentence as a predicate, telling what someone or something is experiencing or characterized by. In the Old Testament, it occurs 72 times, so its use extends across many passages rather than belonging to only one situation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose ordinary meaning cannot be stated confidently from the available lexical information. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Samuel 8:13, but no explicit definition or English rendering is available here. The reference identifies where it occurs, not what the word means by itself. Its precise sense therefore requires the verse text and surrounding context.

Tob is the name of a place or region. It functions as a proper place-name rather than describing a quality such as goodness. In the Old Testament, it appears four times, all in Judges and 2 Samuel, and is consistently rendered “Tob.” The name is connected with events involving Jephthah and later with the Ammonites’ preparations for conflict. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “labour,” the effort expended in carrying out a task. It names human exertion and can describe what people undertake, endure, or possess as the result of their efforts. It occurs 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it expresses a recurring biblical idea rather than a rare technical term. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Jubal is a personal name, identifying a particular man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 4:21, and is rendered “Jubal.” Because it functions as a name, its meaning here is primarily identifying: it points to the person called Jubal. The surrounding verse gives the context for his role, while the word itself serves as his name.

Jaanai is a Hebrew personal name, identifying an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or object. It occurs once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in 1 Chronicles 5:12. Since it functions as a name, its significance here is the person it identifies, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about that person. The name is rendered “Jaanai” in the cited translation.

This Hebrew verb means “spread,” describing an action in which something is spread. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, object, or place. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Esther, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its central meaning remains consistent across these uses, while the surrounding sentence identifies what is spread and how the action relates to the passage. The precise force in a particular verse depends on that surrounding context.

This Hebrew word is a personal name appearing once in the Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:36. The available information identifies the Hebrew name but does not provide a gloss, definition, translation, or verse text that explains what the name itself means. Therefore, its safest plain-language sense is simply the name of a person, while any deeper meaning would require additional scriptural or lexical evidence. Its occurrence is limited to this single reference.

Chileab is a personal name, referring to one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament. It is not presented with an explicit definition or descriptive gloss, so its ordinary lexical meaning cannot be stated beyond recognizing it as a name. The name occurs once, in 2 Samuel 3:3. English renderings preserve it as “Chileab,” rather than translating it into a descriptive phrase. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

Chislon is a Hebrew proper name, rendered “Chislon,” rather than an ordinary word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Numbers 34:21. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the person’s role. Its precise significance in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding biblical passage, not on an added meaning for the name itself.

Abital is a personal name, functioning as the identifying name of an individual rather than as a common word with a stated descriptive meaning. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, and both English renderings preserve it as “Abital.” Because no short definition or gloss is provided, its significance here is its role as a proper name; the surrounding verse is needed for any passage-specific explanation.

This Hebrew word means “herald,” referring to a person who publicly announces a message or command. It functions as a noun and appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 3:4. Its limited occurrence means the word’s broader range cannot be established from repeated biblical usage, but its basic sense is clear: an official announcer who communicates something publicly on behalf of another. The surrounding verse provides the specific setting for its use.

This Hebrew verb describes breaking or reducing something into “pieces.” It presents an action done to an object, rather than naming the object itself. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 17 times, and its uses range across physical things and wider acts of destruction. The central idea remains that something is broken apart so that it no longer remains whole. Its exact force in any verse depends on what is being acted upon and the surrounding sentence.

Luhith is the name of a place mentioned in the Old Testament. It functions as a geographical name rather than a general description or action. The name appears three times, in two verses: once in Isaiah and twice in Jeremiah. Its role is to identify a location connected with the movements and cries described in those passages, while the precise significance of the place in each verse depends on the surrounding verse text. English Bibles render this name as "Luhith".

In the Old Testament, it is especially associated with Israel’s worship, offerings, appointed times, and occasions when God gives commands or meets with his people. It occurs 223 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that gathering and appointed assembly are recurring scriptural ideas.

e.t: Abinoam is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a specific man in the book of Judges. It functions as a proper name rather than a general description or action word. The name occurs four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, each occurrence appearing in Judges. It identifies the father of Barak and is connected with speeches and commands involving him. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic role is to name this individual.

e.t: Mahlah is a Hebrew personal name, referring to a woman rather than describing an action, object, or quality. It is rendered “Mahlah” in the English references and occurs five times in the Hebrew Old Testament. The name appears in several passages concerning the same named person and is also connected with a genealogical birth record. Its meaning here is therefore chiefly identifying: it marks Mahlah as an individual within Israel’s recorded family history.

Matri is a personal name, rendered “Matri,” rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Samuel 10:21. In that verse, it identifies a person, while the verse text and surrounding passage are needed to explain that scene more fully. Its normal meaning is therefore the name Matri, not a broader English concept. The name itself does not provide a separate description or action.

This Hebrew adjective means “full.” It describes a person, object, or situation as possessing its complete measure or contents, rather than being empty or lacking what belongs there. It occurs 58 times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, often describing material fullness, though its precise force depends on the noun or situation it modifies. Genesis 23:9 and Numbers 7 show this ordinary use. In these passages, the word functions as a description of fullness.

This Hebrew word refers to a thing, matter, or stated subject. It is used as a noun for something being discussed, reported, remembered, or considered, rather than naming a specific object every time. In its Old Testament usage, it occurs 24 times, all in Daniel, where it commonly identifies the subject of a conversation or declaration. Its basic sense remains broad: a thing or matter under discussion. The precise reference depends on the surrounding sentence, but the word itself points to the subject being spoken about.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “basins,” containers used among the furnishings connected with worship. It appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in descriptions of the tabernacle furnishings and in a later account concerning temple vessels. The word functions as the object of actions involving making and handling these items, showing that it names a physical object rather than an action or quality. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and its description of the sacred furnishings.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “cave,” referring to a natural hollow or underground place. It is used across the Old Testament for a physical location, and its 38 occurrences show that this is an established everyday noun rather than a rare or specialized expression. The word appears in passages from Genesis through Ezekiel, including references associated with burial places, hiding places, and other locations described as caves.

Marah is a Hebrew proper name for a place, not a general word describing an action or quality. It appears five times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in Exodus and Numbers. The name is consistently rendered “Marah,” so that approved meaning term is best retained rather than expanded with an unsupported synonym. Its use is connected with naming and identifying the place in the biblical journey accounts, while the precise significance of the name in any particular verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

This Hebrew word refers to “morning,” identifying the beginning part of the day. It functions as a time expression rather than describing an action, person, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Psalm 110:3. Because the available wording is limited to this single occurrence and no surrounding verse text is provided here, the word’s broader contextual force should be understood from the passage itself. Its basic lexical sense remains “morning.”

This Hebrew expression refers to a specific term whose precise English meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in 2 Samuel 8:1. The wording functions as an expression rather than a clearly defined everyday action or quality. Its exact sense must therefore remain tied to the wording and broader context of that verse, rather than being expanded into an unsupported translation or interpretation.

Naharai is a personal name, not a general word describing an action, object, or quality. It identifies one individual in the Hebrew Old Testament and appears twice, in 2 Samuel 23:37 and 1 Chronicles 11:39. The available English rendering preserves the name as “Naharai,” so no broader lexical meaning is established here. These are its only two Hebrew occurrences, and its precise significance must be distinguished from meaning supplied by surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “cubits,” a unit used to state the length, width, or height of something. It appears four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, in two verses: Ezra 6:3 and Daniel 3:1. In each case, it functions as a measurement term, helping describe the physical dimensions of a building or object. Its meaning is therefore practical and precise: it identifies the amount of length being measured rather than naming a person, action, or quality.

This Hebrew word expresses “moved.” As an action word, it describes someone being moved toward a response or course of action rather than naming an object. Across its 18 Old Testament occurrences, it appears in settings involving influence or movement. It can function as the main action connecting a person or power with the one affected. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a “tabernacle,” functioning as a noun that names a thing. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Amos 5:26. Because it appears only once and no verse text is available here, its broader use cannot be established from this word record alone. Its basic sense is therefore the named object, “tabernacle,” while the surrounding passage supplies the specific force of the reference.

The Hebrew word means “perverts.” It is an action word: it describes making something depart from what is proper or just, rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Old Testament corpus, it occurs seven times, including laws about judgment and wisdom passages. Its precise force in any one verse depends on what is being affected, but its central idea is wrongful distortion or turning aside.

This Hebrew word means “perverse.” It functions as a descriptive term, presenting something as perverse rather than naming a person, place, or action by itself. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Isaiah 19:14. That single occurrence identifies its basic sense, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what it describes there. The word’s normal force is therefore concise: it marks something as perverse within the sentence where it occurs.

Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding wording.

It is therefore a concrete nature word rather than a broad term for danger, death, or destruction.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “misery,” or to “miseries” when describing such troubles collectively. It names a condition of distress that can be spoken about, seen, or heard before God. The word occurs 36 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad use for human affliction rather than a term limited to one event. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “naked.” It functions as a describing word, identifying a person or people as naked rather than naming an action. It appears 16 times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, across 15 verses, from Genesis through Micah. The English rendering is consistently “naked” in the available translations, supporting this straightforward sense. Its exact force in any verse belongs to that verse’s surrounding context.

Punon is a place-name, rendered as “Punon,” rather than an ordinary descriptive word. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers 33:42–43. The available material identifies it as a named location, but does not provide enough surrounding verse text to explain the location’s identity or significance. Its meaning is therefore the place-name “Punon,” with its specific reference understood from the surrounding biblical context.

This Hebrew word means “judgment.” It names a judicial decision or ruling rather than describing a person, place, or action in general. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Isaiah 28:7, so its normal meaning is supported by that single scriptural occurrence.
